pronunciation.approximation: 'GOON-ur' — a hard g as in 'go', a short full 'u' as in 'put', the n held long and doubled, and the final r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in modern Icelandic Gunnur.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Gunnr is not a theonym built from elements but the common noun itself: gunnr, feminine, 'war, battle' — the valkyrie's name is the thing she governs, personified. The restoration Gunnr keeps the double n and the nominative -r exactly as the manuscripts write them; the name is already plain ASCII, so there is nothing for the restoration to rescue. Tier-2 by rule: no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose.

kin.label: Old Norse

kin.label: Old English cognate
kin.form: gūþ 'war, battle' — the everyday heroic word of Beowulf, the same inherited noun.

kin.label: Old High German cognate
kin.form: gund-, the battle-element in names such as Hildegund.

domains.title: Valkyrie of War
domains.subtitle: Battle Made Divine — the Rider Who Chooses the Slain
domains.lead: Gunnr is the valkyrie whose name is the whole battlefield: Old Norse gunnr is simply the word for war, and the þulur and the Völuspá seeress set her riding among Óðinn's choosers of the slain. Snorri gives her the purest job-description in the corpus: Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and decide battles.

cards.name: The Chosen Slain
cards.desc: The einherjar — the warriors she marks on the field and carries to Valhǫll, the harvest a valkyrie exists to gather.

cards.name: Skuld's Shield
cards.desc: Völuspá's image: Skuld held a shield and Skögul rode with her, and Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul rode behind — the armed company of the god-folk.

cards.name: The War-Spear
cards.desc: The valkyrie's weapon and the battle's own emblem: Snorri says Gunnr, Rota and Skuld ride to every fight to award the victory.

cards.name: The Val-Knot of Choice
cards.desc: The act her office names: val-kjósa, to choose the slain — the divine prerogative of saying who falls and who is taken.

symbols.name: The spear
symbols.meaning: The weapon of the chooser — the stroke that both kills and elects

symbols.name: The shield of the company
symbols.meaning: Völuspá's riding detail: the valkyries go armed and ranked, not as omens but as soldiers

symbols.name: The choice of the slain (valr)
symbols.meaning: The office itself — war's harvest selected by name, the power the name gunnr carries into personhood

symbols.name: The name that is a noun
symbols.meaning: Gunnr the valkyrie and gunnr the battle are one word — war personified walking its own field

mythology.lead: Gunnr has no adventure of her own; her mythology is her office, told in lists that are anything but dry. Three witnesses fix her in the corpus: the Völuspá seeress sees her ride, Snorri states her function in a single sentence, and the þulur keep her name in the valkyrie roll — the tradition's way of saying that battle, in the North, had a chooser, and the chooser had a name.

myths.title: The Riders the Seeress Saw
myths.text: Deep in the völva's vision, between the creation of the world and its burning, the seeress watches the valkyries come: 'She saw valkyries come from far and wide, ready to ride to the gods' people; Skuld held a shield, and Skögul was with her; Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul — now are counted Herjan's ladies, valkyries ready to ride the earth.' Herjan is Óðinn, and the company is his. Gunnr rides fourth-named in the most famous catalogue of the Poetic Edda — not as a character in a story but as a fixture of the cosmos, as certain as the norms and the doom they enforce.

myths.title: The Choosers of the Slain
myths.text: Snorri, explaining Óðinn's household, gives the valkyries their definition and Gunnr her one great sentence: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they allot death to men and award victory. 'Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and to decide the fighting.' The grouping is precise and chilling — two valkyries and a norn riding together, because in Norse thought the choice of the slain and the doom of the slain are the same act seen from two sides. Gunnr's myth is this: war is never random. Someone rides above it. Someone chooses.

myths.title: Kept in the Roll
myths.text: The þulur — the metrical name-lists the skalds learned as their working vocabulary — preserve Gunnr among the heiti of the valkyries, and the same lists hand her name back to poetry as a common noun: gunnr, 'battle', a word a skald could wield in a kenning. The double register is the point. When a skald sang of gunnr, his audience could hear the battle or the battle-maiden in the same syllable, and the tradition never bothered to separate them. The þulur are where 'battle' and 'the valkyrie Battle' are filed under one heading.

lore.syncretism: Gunnr's nearest kin are not borrowings but reflections. Within the Norse corpus she belongs to the tight triad Snorri names — herself, Rota, and the norn Skuld — where the valkyrie's battlefield choice and the norn's weaving of fate are one operation; [[skuld|Skuld]] carries the same office into the world of time itself. Across the sea, the Old English cognate gūþ never grew a person: Beowulf sings of gūþ as plain war, and the personification stayed Norse. Scholars comparing traditions point to the Irish Morrígan and Badb — battle-goddesses who also decide fights and choose their dead — as the closest functional parallel in the neighbouring mythology, though no historical link is provable and none need be claimed. Gunnr needs no foreign template: she is what happens when a warrior culture declines its own word for war in the feminine and gives it a horse.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gunnr's afterlife flows through two channels. The first is the word itself: gunnr lived on as the battle-element of Scandinavian naming — Gunnarr ('warrior of battle'), Gunnhildr ('battle-fight'), and the living Icelandic and Faroese women's name Gunnur — so that the valkyrie's name is still spoken daily in the North, worn by ordinary people. The second is the image she helped fix: the armed maiden riding to the field to choose the dead, the seed from which the whole later figure of the valkyrie grew — the Valkyries of Wagner's Walküre, the shieldmaidens of modern fiction and games, and the revived valkyrie devotion of contemporary Heathenry. In scholarship she stands as the standing example of the Norse habit of personifying abstractions: not an allegory imposed on war, but war itself, named and riding.
lore.extendedMeditation: Gunnr is the most honest figure in the valkyrie roll because she pretends to be nothing but what she is. Other choosers of the slain carry names of tumult, of rulership, of the spear; hers is the field itself. To say that Gunnr chooses the slain is to say that battle chooses its own — that once the spears cross, the outcome belongs to something no combatant commands. The Norse did not soften that thought; they dignified it. They gave the blind lottery of combat a rider, a rank among Óðinn's women, and a place in the seeress's vision, as if to say: what you cannot control, you can at least name. Every soldier who ever marched out knowing the choice was not his own has stood, without knowing it, in Gunnr's shadow.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Gunnr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚴᚢᚾᛦ (k-u-n-R, the k-rune writing g and ᛦ the final nominative -r, the doubled n written with a single rune by runic convention). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: the plain-ASCII gunnr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Gunnr is a wholly textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no cult site is hers — she shares this silence with nearly all the valkyries, who were functions of Óðinn's household rather than objects of cult. The material record knows the office if not the name. Gotlandic picture stones repeatedly show a mounted warrior received by a female figure bearing a drinking horn — the so-called valkyrie-welcome motif — and small female armed figurines, above all the gilt-silver valkyrie with sword and shield found at Hårby on Funen (Denmark), prove the image's currency in the Viking Age. The textual witnesses are the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) for Völuspá and the principal manuscripts of the Prose Edda for Gylfaginning and the þulur; the noun gunnr itself is carved on runestones within personal names, where the battle-element lives on in the anthroponymy.
